title: High Throughput Lipidomic Profiling with High Structural Specificity for Phenotypic Screening
text:
The complete identification of lipids is critical for a better understanding of the roles of lipids in biological
system and diseases. This project aims to develop a next generation lipidomics platform for in-depth lipid
profiling with high structural specificity through advanced mass spectrometry technologies and bioinformatics
pipelines. We anticipate this platform will become a fundamental tool for lipid profiling in biomedical research to
unravel the relationship between lipids and associated functions in biological systems and human health.

title: Genetic regulation of inter- and intra-species microbial community formation
text:
This proposal seeks to mechanistically understand how microorganisms form biofilms, resilient communities of
microbial cells recalcitrant to physical and chemical perturbations. We seek to determine how these microbial
communities are regulated, how they are built, how their specialized properties are elaborated and maintained,
and how these types of behaviors have evolved. These investigations provide the fundamental framework for
the development of strategies to diagnose, treat, and control biofilm infections in medical settings.

title: Core 1: Shared Resource Core (LCRSRC)
text: Linguistic and Cultural Responsiveness Shared Resource Core (LCRSRC) The CCNY-MSK Partnership continues to grow the LCRSRC for this next Partnership cycle, to respond to the tremendous need to reduce cancer incidence and improve outcomes, and to leverage the great strengths, expertise, and tools of the U54 partners in this area. The LCRSRC’s goal is to provide linguistic support to the U54 Partnership Cores (Research Education, PCORE), Research Projects, and Working Groups (Immunotherapy, Biomedical Engineering, Health Policy, Social Influences and Health), and to build the capacity of U54-connected researchers and community members to reduce differences in cancer outcomes by providing linguistic support for translational research, outreach, education, and navigation. This crucial work leverages the strengths of the CCNY Department of Classical and Modern Languages and Literatures, the CCNY Grove School of Engineering, and the MSK Language Initiatives Program to support the U54.The specific aims of the LCRSR are: 1) to provide research consultation support and training in the selection and/or design of specific linguistically tailored quantitative survey tools, research study materials, educational materials, and practices for the U54 Research Projects, PCORE, and Research Education cores; 2) to assist CCNY, MSK, and community U54 investigators in the design, implementation, and analysis of qualitative research: to provide multilingual facilitation for, and to assist in the translation and transcreation of, focus groups, key informant discussions, and in-depth interviews; 3) To enable U54-linked studies and programs to utilize remote simultaneous medical interpreting (RSMI) (UN-style interpreting) to enable seamless communication between community members, patients, researchers, and PCORE, including for precision prevention/medicine and immunotherapy (a) to utilize this resource to help enable MSK Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (IMPACT) genomics studies to engage patients who speak English less than very well at community cancer centers and facilitate genetic testing and shared decision making, (b) to utilize RSMI to help engage community members in clinical trials, precision screening and prevention, and immunotherapy education, services, and studies, (c) to continuously monitor the promise of Artificial Intelligence (AI), e.g., deep learning and Large-Language Models (LLMs), as a medical Interpretation resource, with its potential efficiencies of scale and capacity for almost unlimited dissemination, and 4) to support the implementation of the CCNY Minor/Major in Medical Interpretation and Translation, to give bilingual CCNY students the skills to provide interpretation and translation services for cancer outreach, education, service delivery, and research, and to further build the LCRSRC capacity in these areas. The LCRSR will improve the way that translational cancer research activities and services reflect our surrounding communities, our city, and ultimately, through model dissemination, the nation.

title: Leadership, Planning and Evaluation
text: The senior leadership of the City of Hope Comprehensive Cancer Center (COHCCC) is composed of highly qualified members who bring their respective strengths and unique backgrounds to drive the progress of the center. It is led by John D. Carpten, PhD, Director, a Deputy Director, and eight Associate Directors in the domains of Basic Sciences, Clinical Sciences, Population Sciences, Community Outreach and Engagement, Data Science, Education and Training, Shared Resources, and Administration. With their distinct qualifications, members have worked individually or in collaboration to expand the center, reach new milestones, and further benefit our Catchment Area. COHCCC leadership has a wide array of advisory input to assist in planning for the Center's next steps and evaluating the outcomes of Center programs and policy implementation. Internal advisors include Program and Shared Resource leaders, oversight committees, and the chairs of clinical and research departments, all of whom contribute to shaping our future direction through internal evaluation processes. Our External Advisory Board continues to play a significant role in reviewing our strategic plans and advising on our course of action. We have responded to their recommendations and by virtue of their guidance have 1) integrated the faculty and the shared / genomic resources of TGen within the COHCCC membership, 2) restructured and enhanced our Mass Spectrometry Shared Resource, 3) established the Department of Diabetes and Cancer Metabolism, and 4) initiated the Integrated Drug Development Venture to accelerate translation of scientific discoveries to first-in-human trials. External relationships are also fostered by Community Outreach and Engagement, which has established partnerships between our scientific researchers and organizations that support engagement of populations throughout our Catchment Area. Strategic planning is critical to the development of future programs that advance COHCCC priorities, detailing how we will execute our unwavering commitment to drive paradigm shifts to more effectively prevent, diagnose, and treat cancer. Because of the innovative structure of our institution as a stand-alone cancer center, we are uniquely positioned to realize breakthrough advances in basic science, clinical trials, and patient care. COHCCC engages in a 5-year strategic planning process involving many collaborating partners, including COHCCC faculty, staff, patients, and stakeholders, each providing crucial input and valuable feedback. The approach includes data collection and analysis, multiple interviews with key parties, and an iterative review and approval process of the final deliverable. A new plan was launched in October 2021 with an emphasis on 1) Precision Medicine, 2) Cellular Therapeutics, 3) Access to Cancer Care, and 4) Clinical Networks. Performance and progress of the stated goals within the plan are tracked and catalogued on an ongoing basis.

title: Testing a multistage model of risk factors for cannabis use utilizing a measurement burst design
text: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is most prevalent in young adulthood (ages 18-25) and rates of CUD have increased dramatically in the past decade among young adults; however, there is a paucity of interventions for CUD, highlighting the need for research identifying intervention targets. Existing studies have provided mixed evidence for two event-level risk processes for CU: positive reinforcement (e.g., using to increase positive emotions) and negative reinforcement (e.g., using to decrease negative emotions); however, our preliminary results and the multistage model of substance use provide a potential explanation for these mixed findings by suggesting that these two sets of risk factors may be relevant at different stages of CUD, with positive reinforcement most relevant when CUD symptoms are absent to mild and negative reinforcement becoming prominent when CUD symptoms become more severe. To address existing mixed evidence for event-level risk processes contributing to CU, we aim to accomplish three specific aims using a measurement burst design (i.e., 5 semi-annual bursts of 14-days with 2 surveys per day) with a sample of young adults: 1) identify changes in the effects of positive reinforcement event-level risk factors on CU as CUD develops, 2) test for changes in the effects of negative reinforcement event-level risk factors on CU as CUD develops, and 3) examine associations between trajectories of CU frequency over a 2 year period and the likelihood of having CUD at the final wave of data collection.

title: Computational design and development of small protein inhibitors
text:
This research addresses a critical, relevant public health concern as it will provide a platform to develop new
antivirals that can target type I fusion proteins, which we are applying to the highly pathogenic viruses SARS-
CoV-2, RSV, Nipah virus and MERS. This new class of antivirals is based on small, highly stable computationally
designed proteins. A tight coupling between computation and experiments will also allow the development of
data-driven protein design algorithms.

title: Targeting metabolic dependencies in ZFTA-RELA fusion childhood ependymomas
text:
Ependymomas bearing ZFTA-RELA fusions in children carry a dismal prognosis and have no effective
treatments. Our goal is to unravel how ZFTA-RELA drives epigenetic and metabolic pathways in these tumors.
We aim to target metabolic pathways to develop treatments for this deadly childhood brain cancer.

title: Open-source Low-field MRI: Learn, Design, Build, Scan
text:
We propose a three-day workshop, “Open-source Low-field MRI: Learn, Design, Build, Scan,” to train the next
generation of biomedical imaging scientists through hands-on, open-source, and system-level education in MRI.
This immersive program directly aligns with NIBIB’s mission to advance imaging technologies and NINDS’s goals
in workforce development and open neuroimaging by enabling participants to design, build, and use low-field
MRI systems using reproducible, AI-enabled, and accessible methods. Anchored in proven educational models
and building on a recent successful demonstration, this workshop fosters sustainable community engagement
and provides reusable resources that strengthen the biomedical research enterprise.

title: Project 1: Phospholipid Remodeling in Ferroptosis and Cancer
text:
Success of the proposed study will lead to an in-depth understanding of the molecular basis of ferroptosis
and its interplay with lipid metabolism, and provide insights into the development of novel, mechanism-based
cancer therapies.

title: Statistical and Machine Learning Methods to Address Biomedical Challenges for Integrating Multi-view Data
text:
B PROJECT NARRATIVE
This proposed research is expected to lay the foundation for advances in disease diagnosis, treatment, and
prevention through the integration and interpretation of cross-sectional and longitudinal data from multiple sources.
It will provide a mechanistic understanding of disease interactions, potentially enable discovery of causal biomarkers
and therapeutic targets, enhance patient stratification via endotyping which links subtypes to specific functional and
biological mechanisms, and help address the lack of accessible computational tools and software for extracting new
knowledge in biological systems.

title: Targeting non-genetic and genetic mechanisms to overcome drug resistance in acute myeloid leukemia
text:
Most leukemia patients eventually succumb to their disease due to resistance to both conventional
chemotherapy and innovative targeted therapy. To understand the molecular basis of resistance, we will
integrate phenotypic data obtained from our functional approach to genotypic abnormalities identified using
unbiased approaches. To identify effective treatments for drug-resistant leukemia models, we will take a
broadly applicable functional approach to precision medicine, dynamic BH3 profiling, that measures the
readiness of cells to undergo cell death (apoptosis) in response to drug therapies.

title: Effects of Iron Accumulation in Intracortical Implants and Protection by Iron Chelation
text:
Microelectrodes implanted in the brain are critical tools for recording and stimulation in neuromodulation
approaches to treat a variety of neurological conditions, however, poor long-term stability and functional
performance limit their clinical application. The objective of this proposal is to develop iron chelation as a
therapeutic approach in intracortical implants, understand the effects of iron accumulation at electrode sites on
microglia and neuron degeneration and its impact on electrophysiological signals. Further, the proposal will
determine an optimum iron chelator and develop a microelectrode array platform for local delivery of iron
chelators at the electrode tissue interface to improve long-term functionality of implanted electrodes.

title: Defining Stat3 Antimicrobial Mechanisms in Human Urothelium
text:
Urinary tract infections (UTI) impact millions of individuals annually, with a much better understanding of host
antimicrobial mechanisms required in order to yield much needed alternatives to antibiotics for UTI prevention
and treatment. In this application, using gene editing and next-generation sequencing technology, I will test the
hypothesis that the urothelial transcription factor, STAT3, and its downstream transcriptional targets contribute
to UTI defense in human urothelium. Completion of the proposed aims will identify the mechanisms by which
STAT3 confers host immunity against UTI and reveal STAT3 transcriptional targets to harness for future non-
antibiotic based therapies.

title: Structural and Functional Studies on Proton-activated Chloride (PAC) Channel
text:
The activation of proton-activated chloride channel (PAC) is one of the key factors that determines the severity
of brain damage after ischemic stroke. The proposed study aims to elucidate the working mechanism of how
PAC senses environmental pH and its pharmacological properties. This knowledge will serve as a foundation
to develop novel treatment strategies for ischemic stroke and other diseases that are associated with tissue
acidosis.

title: Genetics of chronotype and impact on metabolic disease
text:
Morningness and eveningness are common traits, but little is known about how these changes reflecting internal
circadian rhythm are caused at the molecular level, and how genetic variation in chronotype relates to metabolic
disease. We will use human genetics and functional assays to understand the role of known and newly identified
genes that contribute to differences in chronotype among individuals, and genetic relationship to diabetes. This
work should inform knowledge of causes of morningness and eveningness, their link to metabolism and is
relevant for leading to better prevention, diagnosis and therapies for circadian disorders and type 2 diabetes.

title: NOT-DA-21-033 Investigation of the neurobiological mechanisms that mediate fentanyl-induced elevations in risk taking in rats
text:
Opioid use disorder is a costly and debilitating condition that is associated with poor decision making and
elevated risk taking, which may increase the risk to relapse; however, the neural mechanisms mediating these
opioid-associated decision making deficits are relatively unknown. The proposed research will use a rat model
to determine how the neural circuitry underlying risk taking becomes compromised following chronic self-
administration of the synthetic opioid fentanyl. Findings from the proposed experiments may reveal tractable
strategies to improve decision making following synthetic opioid use, with the ultimate goal of reducing drug use
and preventing relapse.

title: Machine Learning and Multiomics for Predictive Models and Biomarker Discovery in Preterm Infants.
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as prematurity is a major problem globally and the results of
this research have the potential to improve preterm survival and decrease morbidity. We propose to predict
survival and morbidity, reliably and early in preterm infants using clinical and multi-omics data, which will
enable us to intervene early, improve survival and decrease complications of prematurity (targeted precision
medicine).

title: Augmenting Lysosomal Proteases as a Therapeutic Strategy to Mitigate TDP-43 Pathology in ALS and FTD
text:
This research project aims to develop new treatments for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and
frontotemporal dementia (FTD), which are devastating neurodegenerative disorders. Specifically, we will
determine whether enhancing the activity of the lysosomal proteases - cathepsin B, cathepsin D, and
asparaginyl endopeptidase - within neurons can facilitate the clearance of TDP-43, a protein that accumulates
abnormally in the brains of most patients with ALS and many patients with FTD. By using advanced stem cell
models and analyzing the effects of these enzymes at a molecular level, we hope to identify promising new
therapeutic targets for these currently incurable diseases.

title: Nanoscale Coordination Polymers of Cyclic-di-nucleotides and Peptide Antigens for Effective Therapy of Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
text:
This proposal is relevant to public health because our goal is to create a viable drug candidate that can
improve the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, which is currently associated with very high rates of
morbidity and mortality. The proposed project has the potential to provide a clinical candidate for enhanced
immunotherapy of metastatic colorectal cancer, and this could make the difference in many lives.

title: Computational laminar MRI for diagnosing preclinical and prodromal Alzheimer's disease
text:
In this project, the applicant will develop deep learning models to super-resolve and segment cortical and
hippocampal laminae in longitudinal MRI, enabling investigation of laminar degeneration in Alzheimers disease
(AD). The ﬁndings will enhance understanding of atrophy progression in AD and facilitate the discovery of
novel laminar MRI biomarkers that complement existing structural MRI and PET markers. By improving early
diagnosis of preclinical and prodromal AD at no additional cost, this work will particularly beneﬁt underserved
populations.
